questions.stem: When is a force exerted on a wire in a magnetic field?

options.text: when the wire carries a current
options.explanation: The motor effect needs a current for the wire's own field.

options.text: whenever the wire is made of copper
options.explanation: Material is irrelevant; the current matters.

options.text: only when the wire is still and disconnected
options.explanation: Without current there is no motor effect.

options.text: only when the field is switched off
options.explanation: The field is a required ingredient, not an obstacle.

questions.stem: The motor effect arises because:

options.text: the current leaks into the magnet
options.explanation: No charge crosses into the magnet.

options.text: the wire's field and the magnet's field combine unevenly around the wire
options.explanation: Reinforcement on one side and cancellation on the other give the sideways force.

options.text: the wire heats up and expands
options.explanation: Heating is real but is not the force mechanism.

options.text: the magnet attracts the copper atoms
options.explanation: Copper is non-magnetic; attraction is not the mechanism.

questions.stem: The force on a current-carrying wire in a field acts:

options.text: along the field lines
options.explanation: The force is perpendicular to the field, not along it.

options.text: vertically upwards always
options.explanation: Direction depends on current and field directions.

options.text: perpendicular to both the current and the field
options.explanation: The force is at right angles to both inputs.

options.text: along the wire, pushing the current faster
options.explanation: The force is sideways to the current, not along it.

questions.stem: Both the current and the magnetic field are reversed. What happens to the force?

options.text: it reverses
options.explanation: One reversal flips the force; two restore it.

options.text: it doubles
options.explanation: Reversals change direction, not magnitude.

options.text: it disappears
options.explanation: The force persists with unchanged direction.

options.text: it stays in the same direction
options.explanation: Two reversals cancel: the force direction is unchanged.

questions.stem: Which devices apply the motor effect?

options.text: d.c. electric motors and loudspeakers
options.explanation: Both convert current plus field into force and motion.

options.text: transformers and dynamos
options.explanation: Those apply induction, the inverse effect.

options.text: electromagnets and relays
options.explanation: Those apply the field produced by current, not the force on it.

options.text: thermometers and barometers
options.explanation: Neither involves magnetic forces.

questions.stem: State the name of the effect where a current-carrying wire experiences a force in a magnetic field.
questions.modelAnswer: It is called the motor effect, seen when a current-carrying wire lies in a magnetic field.

questions.stem: State what happens to the force on a wire if only the magnetic field is reversed.
questions.modelAnswer: The force reverses direction because it depends on the field direction.

questions.stem: Explain why a current-carrying wire experiences a force between magnet poles.
questions.modelAnswer: The wire's own circular field adds to the magnet's uniform field: on one side of the wire the two fields reinforce into a strong region, and on the other side they cancel into a weak one. The field then behaves like a stretched catapult line, pushing the wire from the strong side towards the weak side — a force perpendicular to both the current and the field.

questions.stem: A wire between poles feels an upward force. Predict the new force direction if (a) the current is reversed, (b) the current is reversed AND the poles are swapped.
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Reversing only the current flips the force to downwards. (b) Reversing both the current and the field flips the force twice, so it is upwards again — unchanged.

questions.stem: Why do the two horizontal sides of the motor coil feel opposite forces?

options.text: the commutator pushes one side up
options.explanation: The commutator feeds current; the field provides the forces.

options.text: their currents flow in opposite directions
options.explanation: Antiparallel currents in the same field feel antiparallel forces.

options.text: they are made of different metals
options.explanation: Both sides are the same coil of wire.

options.text: the field is stronger on one side only
options.explanation: The field is uniform between the poles; the currents differ.

questions.stem: What is the role of the split-ring commutator in a d.c. motor?

options.text: it measures the coil's speed
options.explanation: The commutator is a contact, not a sensor.

options.text: it reduces the coil's resistance
options.explanation: Its function is the current swap, not resistance control.

options.text: it reverses the coil's current every half turn
options.explanation: The swap keeps the torque in one rotational sense.

options.text: it reverses the magnet's poles every half turn
options.explanation: The poles stay fixed; the current is what flips.

questions.stem: The current to a spinning motor coil is switched off at the top of a turn. What happens?

options.text: the coil keeps spinning at constant speed forever
options.explanation: Friction slows it — nothing sustains the rotation.

options.text: the coil reverses direction
options.explanation: Without forces nothing reverses the rotation.

options.text: the coil jumps off the axle
options.explanation: No force acts to eject the coil.

options.text: the coil slows and stops, with no forces to sustain rotation
options.explanation: No current means no motor-effect forces.

questions.stem: Which change makes a d.c. motor spin FASTER?

options.text: increasing the current through the coil
options.explanation: Bigger current, bigger forces, faster rotation.

options.text: decreasing the magnetic field strength
options.explanation: Weaker field gives smaller forces and slower spin.

options.text: removing half the coil's turns
options.explanation: Fewer turns reduce the total force on the coil.

options.text: insulating the coil from the commutator
options.explanation: That cuts the current entirely — the motor stops.

questions.stem: The poles of a running motor are swapped. What happens to the rotation?

options.text: the coil spins faster
options.explanation: Field swap changes direction, not magnitude.

options.text: the coil spins the opposite way
options.explanation: Both forces flip, so the torque reverses.

options.text: the coil keeps spinning the same way
options.explanation: The force directions both reverse with the field.

options.text: the coil stops immediately
options.explanation: The forces still act — now in the opposite rotational sense.

questions.stem: State the two forces that act on a motor coil's horizontal sides.
questions.modelAnswer: One side feels an upward force and the other side feels a downward force, forming a turning couple.

questions.stem: State why the coil continues rotating past the vertical position.
questions.modelAnswer: The split-ring commutator reverses the current every half turn, so the forces keep pushing the coil round in the same rotational sense.

questions.stem: Explain how opposite currents on the two sides of a coil produce rotation.
questions.modelAnswer: In the same magnetic field, the two horizontal sides carry currents in opposite directions, so the motor effect gives them forces in opposite vertical directions — one up, one down. Because the forces act on opposite sides of the axle they form a couple, and a couple produces rotation of the coil rather than translation.

questions.stem: A model motor spins sluggishly. List three independent adjustments that would increase its speed, each justified by the motor effect.
questions.modelAnswer: Increase the current — each side's force grows with current. Use stronger magnets — a stronger field gives larger forces on the same current. Add more turns to the coil — more current-carrying sides contribute force, increasing the couple. Any of these raises the torque and the spin rate.

questions.stem: What is the turning effect on the coil when it stands vertical in the field?

options.text: reversed — the coil begins spinning backwards
options.explanation: No turning force exists at that instant to reverse anything.

options.text: doubled by the commutator
options.explanation: The commutator swaps current; it does not amplify force.

options.text: zero — the forces no longer form a turning couple
options.explanation: The forces act towards the axle at the vertical position.

options.text: maximum — the coil turns fastest here
options.explanation: The couple is smallest at vertical, not largest.

questions.stem: Why must the current be reversed as the coil passes the vertical position?

options.text: to reduce the current for safety
options.explanation: The swap is about direction, not magnitude or safety.

options.text: because the coil's resistance changes at vertical
options.explanation: Resistance does not step-change at the vertical position.

options.text: to let the coil cool down
options.explanation: Cooling is irrelevant to the half-turn geometry.

options.text: so the forces keep driving the same rotation after the sides swap places
options.explanation: The reversal re-aligns the forces with the rotation.

questions.stem: A motor runs WITHOUT a commutator. Predict its behaviour.

options.text: it turns to the horizontal position and settles there
options.explanation: Past vertical the forces oppose rotation and hold the coil horizontal.

options.text: it spins continuously in one direction
options.explanation: Past vertical the forces reverse the torque.

options.text: it spins faster and faster
options.explanation: Nothing accelerates it beyond the initial couple.

options.text: it vibrates on the spot
options.explanation: The torque pulls it to rest at horizontal, not into vibration.

questions.stem: After a 180° rotation, the current is unchanged (no commutator). The force on each side now acts:

options.text: there is no force any more
options.explanation: Current and field persist, so the forces persist.

options.text: opposite to the rotation, resisting it
options.explanation: The sides swapped positions, so the same currents now give opposing forces.

options.text: in the direction of rotation
options.explanation: That was true before the half turn, not after.

options.text: vertically, with no horizontal component
options.explanation: The forces stay vertical but their turning sense flips.

questions.stem: Which statement about the vertical position is correct?

options.text: the forces double
options.explanation: Nothing doubles at the vertical orientation.

options.text: the field switches off
options.explanation: The magnets' field is unchanged by coil position.

options.text: the forces on the sides still exist but produce no rotation
options.explanation: Forces persist; their lines of action pass through the axle region.

options.text: the forces disappear because the current is zero
options.explanation: The current flows — the commutator bridges the gap.

questions.stem: State the forces' turning effect on the vertical coil.
questions.modelAnswer: The forces act towards the axle and produce no turning effect on the coil.

questions.stem: State what the commutator does at the vertical position.
questions.modelAnswer: The split ring reverses the current in the coil at the vertical position.

questions.stem: Explain why, without a commutator, a motor coil ends up resting horizontally.
questions.modelAnswer: Past the vertical position each side occupies the place the other just left, so with an unchanged current the motor-effect forces now act the opposite way round — one side pushed where it was pulled before. The resulting couple opposes the rotation, swings the coil back, and the coil settles in the horizontal orientation where the forces are balanced as a turning couple is absent there too.

questions.stem: A motor's split ring is fitted half a turn out of phase. Predict the motion and justify it.
questions.modelAnswer: The current reverses at the horizontal instead of the vertical position, so for part of each turn the forces oppose the rotation. The coil jerks, loses most of its torque, and either crawls round unevenly or settles stuck — the swap must be synchronised with the vertical dead-centre for smooth rotation.

questions.stem: What does the force on a loudspeaker's coil do to the cone?

options.text: it spins the cone like a fan
options.explanation: The radial field gives axial forces, not rotation.

options.text: it heats the cone to emit sound
options.explanation: Sound comes from cone vibration, not heat.

options.text: it holds the cone perfectly still
options.explanation: A still cone makes no sound.

options.text: it moves the cone in and out along its axis
options.explanation: The alternating force vibrates the cone.

questions.stem: Why does a loudspeaker cone vibrate?

options.text: the alternating current reverses the force direction rapidly
options.explanation: Each reversal swaps the push for a pull on the coil.

options.text: the magnet switches its poles on and off
options.explanation: The permanent magnet's poles stay fixed.

options.text: air blows through the coil
options.explanation: Air movement is the output, not the driver.

options.text: the coil's resistance oscillates
options.explanation: The signal varies the current, not the resistance.

questions.stem: The current through a speaker coil is increased. What happens to the force and the sound?

options.text: no change to either
options.explanation: The force tracks the current directly.

options.text: bigger force, louder sound
options.explanation: Force grows with current; larger cone swings make louder sound.

options.text: smaller force, quieter sound
options.explanation: That inverts the current–force link.

options.text: same force, higher pitch
options.explanation: Current size changes loudness, not frequency.

questions.stem: A loudspeaker magnet is swapped for a stronger one. What changes?

options.text: the force direction reverses
options.explanation: Strength changes magnitude, not direction.

options.text: the coil stops responding to current
options.explanation: The coil responds even more strongly.

options.text: the forces on the coil grow for the same current
options.explanation: Force scales with field strength.

options.text: the forces shrink
options.explanation: A stronger field gives larger forces.

questions.stem: The connections to a speaker are swapped over, reversing the current direction. What happens to the cone's vibration?

options.text: the cone stops vibrating
options.explanation: The alternating current still alternates the force.

options.text: the cone vibrates twice as fast
options.explanation: Frequency follows the signal, which is unchanged.

options.text: the sound becomes louder
options.explanation: Loudness tracks force size, which is unchanged.

options.text: each push becomes a pull, so the vibration is inverted but sound continues
options.explanation: The force reverses; the alternating pattern just mirrors.

questions.stem: State what provides the magnetic field in a loudspeaker.
questions.modelAnswer: A permanent magnet provides the field in which the coil sits.

questions.stem: State the two quantities the motor-effect force increases with.
questions.modelAnswer: The force increases with the current and with the strength of the magnetic field.

questions.stem: Explain why the loudspeaker cone reproduces the waveform of the audio signal.
questions.modelAnswer: The force on the coil tracks the audio current: it grows and shrinks with the signal's size and reverses whenever the signal reverses direction. The cone is driven by that force, so its displacement rises, falls and reverses in step with the signal — tracing the same waveform and recreating the recorded pressure pattern as sound.

questions.stem: A demonstration speaker is built with a weaker magnet and then a stronger one, all else equal. Compare the cone's motion and the sound in the two cases.
questions.modelAnswer: With the weaker magnet the force on the coil for the same signal current is smaller, so the cone swings a shorter distance each vibration and the sound is quieter. With the stronger magnet the same signal gives larger forces, wider cone swings and louder sound — the vibration frequency is set by the signal and stays the same in both cases.
